source.title: Descriptive Collision in Sparse Autoencoder Auto-Interpretability: When One Explanation Describes Many Features

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses interpretability explanations and their ability to identify features, but its empirical analysis is about reuse of human-written labels for SAE features. It does not test the neuron-pole claims or the specific tests described in V1–V7.
record.gate_note: The study reanalyzes labels on SAE features, not neuron poles or neuron-level explanations. Its collision results do not test whether a single neuron pole has one main job, whether explanations predict firing on held-out text, or whether neuron-based attribution graphs suffice. The paper explicitly says it does not generate new auto-interpretability explanations or evaluate their quality with an LLM judge. Rows below record its related finding about label reuse, not evidence for or against any listed version.
record.test_reason: The study reanalyzes 722 human-written labels on SAE features from Gemma 2 2B and Pythia 70M. It measures label reuse ("descriptive collision"), not whether neuron poles have one main job. It does not measure whether explanations predict firing on new text or score neuron explanations by simulation. It also does not test neuron-based attribution graphs or the InceptionV1 examples. Its argument concerns identifying SAE features from a label, which is a different construct from V6's prediction failure. The authors say they generate no new explanations and run no LLM-judge evaluation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors also prove that detection-style scoring is invariant to collision. They argue machine-generated labels should collide at least as much as human ones, though this is untested.
record.recipe_differences: The study reanalyzes human-written labels for SAE features and proposes collision-sensitive scoring; it does not measure neuron poles or apply the original neuron-explanation evaluation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported collision rates vary by model source: the paper reports descriptive resolution of 61.8% of maximum for Gemma 2 2B and 80.9% for Pythia 70M. It also notes that discrimination scores depend on the choice of discrimination set, but does not test alternative choices.

fits_no_version.finding: In a corpus of 722 expert-annotated SAE features, 82.1% share their label with another feature. 'Plural nouns' labels 101 features across 18 layer/component sites. Labels resolve only 70% of the bits of feature identity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Short natural-language labels for SAE features often describe a property shared by many distinct features, so a label that predicts activations does not identify its feature.

record.problems: The empirical analysis is restricted to one public corpus of 722 human-annotated SAE features and does not measure collision rates for machine-generated explanations. The paper itself says the exact numerical estimates are corpus-specific and leaves large-scale evaluation of machine-generated labels to future work.
record.rows_left_out: No additional collision statistics were extracted beyond the main corpus, model-breakdown, cross-layer, note, and annotation-length results above. The proposed scoring methods are not empirical results on the claim's neuron-pole measures.

untested.parts: All: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job shares (about 90% one job, 7% two, 2–4% not understood).
All: neuron-pole shares across other dense and mixture-of-experts models and scales.
All: InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, and recursive generalization.
All: effect of architecture, regularization and tools on the interpretable-neuron share.
All: neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
All: whether explanations fitting activating examples fail to predict neuron firing on other text. The paper assumes explanations may predict firing and studies identification instead.
All: simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none'] with state cannot_determine. They measure label reuse on SAE features, not neuron poles. Minor inconsistency in the source: the Figure 2 graphic says top-20 covers 49.7%, but the caption says 50.1%. Further unextracted statistics (40.3% of features in clusters of size 10 or more; top-10 labels cover 38.9%) bear on no version. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job counts and the proportions with one job, two related jobs, or jobs not yet understood.
Neuron-pole job shares across models, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and the proposed pose or recursive-generalization account.
Architecture, regularization, tools, and interpretability estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain its behaviour without a trained replacement model.
Whether explanations derived from activating examples fail to predict firing on other examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

relation.reason: Discusses auto-interp labelling limits (citing Bills et al. on neurons) without testing the claim or citing the original essay; discusses fits.

tranche.reason: Reanalyzes reuse of human labels on SAE features (Gemma 2 2B, Pythia 70M). It does not measure neuron-pole job shares, firing prediction on new text, or simulation scores of neuron explanations, so it neither tests nor uses any version.

source_check.notes: All 9 rows match Table 1 and Section 4. They concern SAE-feature label collision, not neuron poles, so cannot_determine and no verdicts are right. The 3.07 mean is 722/235 features per annotation string, not a per-feature average. The paper's per-model counts (470 Gemma + 277 Pythia = 747) don't reconcile with 722 after one duplicate.
